Fixed Width Confidence Interval for a Normal Mean

Source: R/seq_fwd_norm_mean.R
seq_fwd_norm_mean.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential fixed width confidence interval for the mean of a normal population with unknown variance (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009). The aim is an interval of half width d (full width \(2d\)) around the sample mean with the stated confidence level. No fixed sample size can promise that, because the size needed depends on the unknown variance, so observations are collected until the sample size reaches the size the current variance estimate calls for.

Usage

seq_fwd_norm_mean(x, d, conf_level = 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 2).

d

The half width of the confidence interval, in the units of the data: the interval reported is the sample mean plus and minus d, so its full width is \(2d\). A positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level (default 0.95).

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

lower_limit

The sample mean minus d.

mean

The sample mean, the point estimate.

upper_limit

The sample mean plus d.

optimal_n

The sample size the current variance estimate calls for, \(\lceil z_{\alpha/2}^2 S_n^2 / d^2 \rceil\) (NA when the data are constant).

current_n

The number of observations used.

Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE once current_n is at least optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), conf_level, width (the full width \(2d\)), method, variance_unusable (TRUE when the data are constant, so that no variance has been estimated), and notes.

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

With the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) known, the interval \(\bar{X}_n \pm d\) has confidence level \(1 - \alpha\) when \(n \ge n^* = z_{\alpha/2}^2 \sigma^2 / d^2\) (seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal returns that sample size, rounded up to a whole number, for a given variance). The sequential rule replaces \(\sigma^2\) by the sample variance \(S_n^2\): sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) with $$n \ge z_{\alpha/2}^2 S_n^2 / d^2 .$$ The optimal_n row is the right hand side rounded up, evaluated at the current data. The reported interval is always \(\bar{X}_n \pm d\); it has the stated confidence level only once the rule is met.

The confidence level is asymptotic. It is attained in the limit as d shrinks (so that the required sample size grows), not at every d. When the target is wide relative to the standard deviation, sampling tends to stop early on an underestimate of the variance, and coverage falls below the stated level. In simulation (normal data with standard deviation 2, nominal 0.95, the pilot of seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot() with its defaults, which was 10 at every target used, 40,000 replications, Monte Carlo standard error 0.001), coverage was 0.933 at d = 1 (where the required sample size \(n^*\) is about 15). It was lowest, about 0.922, when \(n^*\) was between 24 and 28, and rose from there: 0.930 at \(n^*\) of 40, 0.938 at d = 0.5 (\(n^*\) about 61), 0.943 at \(n^*\) of 100, and 0.949 at d = 0.25 (\(n^*\) about 246; 400,000 replications). The pilot matters: with m_0 = 4 in place of the default 10, coverage at d = 1 was 0.880. ts_fwd_norm_mean is the two stage alternative, whose confidence level is guaranteed for normal data at the price of a larger expected sample size.

Constant data. If every observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value, as with gain scores of 0.3 computed as posttest minus pretest), the sample variance is zero, or nothing but rounding error, and the rule as printed would be met at once. The function departs from the printed rule deliberately: no variance has been estimated, so the rule is reported as not met, optimal_n is NA, attr(out, "variance_unusable") is TRUE, and a note says so (see smsd_check_methods); data whose real spread is that small beside their size should have a common value subtracted first. The limits are still reported (the sample mean minus and plus d, which involve no variance), but they are then not an interval to report: summary(), glance(), and tidy() return them without the note, so test attr(out, "variance_unusable") before using them.

Extreme units. Data that do vary, but whose spread is so large or so small that the sample variance cannot be represented in double precision (differences among the observations beyond about \(10^{154}\) or below about \(10^{-162}\)), are an error that says to change the units. That case is not reported as a rule not yet met, because collecting more data cannot help.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot; seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal for the sample size when the variance is known, the benchmark this procedure aims for; seq_fwd_dfr_mean, which makes no normality assumption; ts_fwd_norm_mean for the two stage procedure.

Other seq_fwd_norm_mean: seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal(), seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean score on a 100 point exam, to within 2 points with 95% confidence.
# Scores are simulated here with a standard deviation of 12.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = 2, conf_level = 0.95)
scores <- rnorm(m, mean = 70, sd = 12)
out <- seq_fwd_norm_mean(scores, d = 2, conf_level = 0.95)
out
#> Sequential check (fixed width interval (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 10
#>   Criterion n     : 126
#>   Target width    : 4
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 64.24481
#>   mean              : 66.24481
#>   upper_limit       : 68.24481
#>   optimal_n         : 126
#>   current_n         : 10
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one student at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  scores <- c(scores, rnorm(1, mean = 70, sd = 12))
  out <- seq_fwd_norm_mean(scores, d = 2, conf_level = 0.95)
}
out
#> Sequential check (fixed width interval (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 146
#>   Criterion n     : 145
#>   Target width    : 4
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 67.16453
#>   mean              : 69.16453
#>   upper_limit       : 71.16453
#>   optimal_n         : 145
#>   current_n         : 146
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
